messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 62
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Psychiatrist
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 47

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Media / News: Related news, Auditory (Language Confusion): Incomprehensible chatter, Authority Figures: People in uniform
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Going Out: Going out, Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Redirection: I think of something else
  Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture, Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down, No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rodrigo is a 62-year-old Latin American psychiatrist who presents for an initial evaluation carrying a history he has spent decades attempting to outrun professionally and personally. He is single, lives alone in a mid-sized American city, and describes his current functioning as "barely adequate." His PCL-5 score of 47 places him in the moderate-to-severe range, and what emerges across the first sessions is a presentation shaped not only by what was done to him, but by the institutional silence that followed.

Approximately thirty years ago, Rodrigo was detained without charge by state security forces in his country of origin. For several weeks he was held in a facility where interrogators spoke in overlapping, deliberately disorienting commands — voices layered over voices, questions answered with questions, language used as a weapon of confusion rather than communication. He was subjected to systematic physical and psychological torture. The men who held him wore uniforms. When he was eventually released, no charges were ever filed, no investigation was opened, and the officers responsible continued in their posts. He emigrated to the United States within a year, completed his psychiatric training here, and built what appeared from the outside to be a successful career. He did not seek treatment.

The memories do not arrive as recollections. When something in his environment triggers them, the full experience returns across every sense simultaneously — the smell of a damp concrete room, the pressure of restraints, the layered unintelligible voices — and it does not feel like remembering. It feels like being there. Some moments of the detention are rendered in excruciating clarity; others are entirely blank, as though those hours were excised. The fragmented, non-linear quality of the memory means that certain triggers bypass any cognitive preparation and deliver him back without warning. A news broadcast covering political detentions in Latin America, heard while he is reviewing patient notes in his office, has done exactly this — the screen's imagery and the reporter's cadence sufficient to collapse the distance between then and now. The news, in this way, does not merely distress him; it reinstates the trauma as present-tense reality.

The appraisals Rodrigo carries are not abstract. He is certain — not afraid, but certain — that the institutions that should have protected him failed him deliberately, and that the men responsible have lived their lives without consequence. This conviction is not merely a painful belief; it functions as a lens through which triggers are interpreted. When he encounters a person in uniform — a security guard at the hospital entrance, a police officer on the street — the sight does not only recall the past. It confirms, in that moment, that the conditions of his harm remain unremedied and that authority is still dangerous. The appraisal of institutional failure and absent accountability sharpens the meaning of each trigger, so that what might otherwise be a neutral encounter becomes evidence of ongoing threat, and the full memory presses forward again.

Over the years, Rodrigo has built an elaborate system of management that he has mistaken for coping. He avoids going out wherever possible, scheduling his clinical work to minimize transit and public exposure. Before any interaction — with colleagues, with patients, with a pharmacist — he rehearses what he will say, running through likely conversational branches to ensure he will not be caught off guard by incomprehensible or overlapping speech. When intrusive content begins to surface, he redirects his attention forcibly to something neutral. Each of these strategies, however, has quietly maintained the problem it was designed to solve. By rehearsing conversations obsessively, he never tests whether unscripted speech is actually dangerous, and the anticipatory anxiety remains intact. By avoiding public space, he has not been able to disconfirm the threat posed by uniforms or crowds, and the triggers remain fully potent. The redirection prevents the memory from being processed and leaves it structurally unchanged, ready to return. His avoidance has also cost him concretely: colleagues have noted his withdrawal, he has declined committee work and conferences, and he has not attended a professional gathering in four years — a man who trained others in trauma care, now unable to sit in a room where he cannot control the exits. The isolation has deepened his sense of having lost his connection to his culture and community, and that loss in turn feeds the appraisal that something irreplaceable was taken from him by people who will never be named.

Rodrigo sought help after a junior resident, during a case presentation, played an audio recording of a patient's disorganized speech. The overlapping, incomprehensible chatter filled the seminar room and Rodrigo left without explanation. He made the referral to himself the same evening. What he is most afraid of is that treatment will require him to say aloud what was done to him. What he most hopes is that it will not always feel this close.
